It pleases God that faith should be in that sense the condition of salvation, that it should be the ground of the distinction made in the consequent state of men, the ground of the distinction between those that are saved and those that perish, those that are happy and those that are miserable. The fitness of the way of salvation, and the beauty of the method of God's dealings with fallen man consequent on the giving a Savior, appears much in his making that great difference among fallen men in bestowing eternal life on such as believe and leaving those eternally to perish who believe not. But the receiving or rejecting Christ could be no ground of this distinction if the elect were first created in heaven and reprobates in hell, for then the difference of their state would be antecedent to [the] difference between them consisting in faith and unbelief.

6. By faith in Christ being exercised before the receiving the reward, believers are prepared for the reward, to receive it sensibly, as from Christ, and to give him the glory of it. In this way they receive it from Christ and as the consequence of their applying to him for it the more sensibly to themselves.

7. If the elect should be first created in the possession of the purchased paradise, there would be no opportunity for those particular exercises of faith in the Redeemer wherein much of the fitness of it to an interest in the Savior and his redemption consists, and which peculiarly tend to make his redemption precious and to give him the proper glory which belongs to him as a Savior. For there would be no opportunity for any proper conviction of sin, for the elect would never be sensible of any sin in themselves, for they never would have sin but would be perfectly sinless in the beginning, and so never would by sense and experience be made sensible of their need of a Savior, nor ever would come to Christ in the proper exercises of repentance and humiliation. Nor would there be any opportunity to honor Christ by the proper exercises of that disposition to prefer Christ to all other things which is contained in true faith. This disposition

<!-- p. 504 -->

could not be exercised and manifested under its proper trials. Persons would have no opportunity to come to him so as to forsake all for him, to go and sell all for the pearl of great price; no opportunity to receive Christ with his cross as well as with his crown; no opportunity to close with Christ and his religion with great labors and sufferings, as sitting down and counting the cost.

8. If man never were in a state of probation under the offers of the Savior, Christ never would have that honor, put upon him by God, that men are required to receive him on pain of God's peculiar wrath. There would be no punishment, nor threatening of punishment, for sinners not accepting Christ. By the terrible punishment of the sin of unbelief and sins against the gospel, God exalts and magnifies the Redeemer and his redemption, tending to impress the minds of saints and angels with a great sense of Christ's high dignity and the exceeding greatness and value of his redeeming grace and love.

9. If men should be born into the world and live here under the offers of Christ, and yet an interest in Christ were not only to [be] obtained in this world but before death and after death indifferently, and this were known, this would vastly encourage men's delay of repentance and turning from sin to God through Christ, and living boldly in the neglect of Christ and of the means of an interest in him, and would exceedingly encourage them to give themselves up to their own lusts.

10. If men should be born into this world, and here was no such thing as the offer of a Savior, or a probation whether they would accept of him or use any means to obtain Christ's benefits, but it was known that those that were to enjoy Christ's benefits were to be sanctified and have their souls united to Christ after death, it would take off almost all restraint on men's lust, make Christ nothing but the minister of sin to embolden them in wickedness and a means in that respect[^046-note1] of turning earth into hell.

11. 'Tis fit that Christ, that was appointed to bruise the serpent's head and destroy the works of the devil, should conquer Satan in his own territories; that he should be overthrown in Christ's actual salvation, wherein he rescues men from his power on the same stage where he seemed to conquer; that he should be destroyed by the second man and head of men in the same world where he destroyed the first head of men; and that the Redeemer should set up his kingdom of grace and salvation in the same world where Satan hath set up his kingdom of sin and misery, that Christ's kingdom should be built on the ruins of Satan's kingdom.

<!-- p. 505 -->

12. 'Tis fit that Christ should be glorified and exalted here in the same stage whereon he was humbled and suffered; that as he was exhibited in meanness and disgrace as a servant under the dominion of his enemies, men and devils, who exercised their dominion and tyranny over him, as it were, in his destruction as their subject and malefactor, so that here he should reign and vanquish his enemies and they should be made his footstool; that as he suffered in the world, in Satan's territories, and by the malignant influences of his domination, so here he should erect a glorious kingdom on the ruins of that dominion of the devil that he so suffered by; and as he suffered as a subject of the kingdom of men, the Roman Empire, the chief monarchy that ever was set up among men, so he should set up a kingdom here on the ruins of that kingdom and over all other kingdoms and nations of mankind.

13. If the application of redemption were not in this world, there would not properly have been any such thing as a conquest of Satan in this application in the conversion of sinners, in the preservation of a saint, and carrying on a work of grace to glory against the utmost power and opposition of Satan. For if the application of redemption were first in heaven, there Satan has nothing to do, and never comes, and has no opportunity to make any opposition. And the glory of Christ's power would have failed in so irresistibly conquering sin, Satan and the world, in beginning, upholding and carrying on the work of grace in the hearts of saints.

14. As Satan set up a kingdom in this world by his subtlety, and by the same means has all along promoted it, so God saw meet that his Son should set up a kingdom, and maintain and promote it in opposition to Satan's kingdom in the exercise [of] wonderful wisdom, that should appear to be infinitely above Satan's wisdom, baffling and confounding him in his most subtle devices, taking him in his own snare, leading him into the pit that he has digged. But occasion and opportunity for this would have failed if the application of redemption were begun in heaven, for then this application would be brought without means wisely to be ordered and disposed, and where Satan has nothing to do, and the marvelous wisdom of God—appearing in his dispensations towards his [church],[^046-note2] the methods of his providence, and of the operations of his Spirit in carrying on the great designs of his kingdom in the world—never would have been seen.

15. God saw fit that sanctification itself and the whole of salvation, excepting the very first act of faith, should be given as the consequence of

<!-- p. 506 -->

faith, and as dependent on it as the condition of all. But if the elect were created in a state of perfect holiness in heaven, this could not have been.

16. If there had [been] no state of probation appointed to precede the reward, there could [not] have been a diversity of degrees of glory established by any such rule (wonderfully manifesting the wisdom of God) as that which now takes place, viz. that the future glory of saints shall be greater or less according to the degrees of holiness and good works and fruits of righteousness, to the glory of God and good of fellow creatures in [an] antecedent state of probation.

17. If union to Christ and sanctification were first begun in heaven, then would have failed those wonderful manifestations of the freeness, independence, riches and immutability of the grace and love of Christ—and his faithfulness in his covenant—that are by the mercy he shows 'em under all their infirmities and failings, unsteadiness and ingratitude, after their conversion.

18. The elect being first in this world in a state of sin and misery—of which they are convinced by the Spirit—and by the experience they have of sin and suffering after conversion, are prepared for a state of perfect holiness and glory. By the knowledge of evil they have the greater and better knowledge of good, and are more sensible of the beauty of holiness, and the value of happiness, and the greatness of the benefit of salvation from sin and misery, and the value and riches of God's grace in bestowing these benefits upon them, who have such experience of their unworthiness and such a taste of what misery they deserve. Experience and sense of sin and misery serves to humble the soul and so to fit it for exaltation.

19. The saints, by the state that they are in in this world and the work they have here to do, are fitted and trained up for the purchased reward. Humbling and self-emptying virtues are exercised (and the sense and habit fixed), such as humility, submission, meekness, patience, forgiveness and obedience to a law properly so called, i.e. commands enforced by threatenings of God's awful displeasure and obedience to difficult commands. And dependence is, in many respects, exercised so as it is not in a state of perfect glory. If holiness were first begun in heaven, there would not be that foundation laid for building it up to so great a height, nor the bringing it to so amiable a beauty in the manner of its exercise, and so no foundation for so sweet a joy.

The things that have been said concerning the necessity of a state and time of probation in this world before the bestowment of the purchased reward are to be understood of the church of the elect collectively, taken[^046-note3]

<!-- p. 507 -->

as a body, rather than of each individual person. As to elect infants that die in infancy, we have less to lead us into an understanding of God's dealings with them than of his dealings with adult persons.

But I would nevertheless observe the following things concerning them:

1. That some of those things that have been mentioned that render existence in an antecedent state necessary before the elect exist in their state of reward in heaven [are applicable to them]. Infants have an antecedent existence, and so are the posterity of Adam, and so are first in a state of sin and misery under guilt and exposed to punishment and destruction, which would never have been if they had first been created in heaven. Elect infants in heaven will fully know they have been in a state of sin and misery, and so will know that they have actually been redeemed out of such a state by Christ.

2. Although infants will not personally and actively have accepted of Christ as their Savior before they are in their state of reward, yet there will be enough to make it visible to angels and visible to the whole assembly of elect creatures that the reward is dependent on faith. For all will see that, with regard to the body or church they belonged to, it is glorified after acceptance of Christ. And their parents' actual faith (which hath influence in the infants' salvation and on the account of which in some sense the infant is saved) will precede the infants' glory. So that the visibility of the suitableness and beauty of the way of salvation in the eye of the heavenly inhabitants and in the eye of infants themselves, consisting in a dependence of eternal life on[^046-note4] faith, will be sufficiently provided for.

3. Glorified infants, being members of a body that has (i.e. in its chief members) actually passed through the trials, exercises and discipline of an antecedent day of probation, and being members of this body in its perfect and glorified state, wherein the union and fellowship of all the members in one body shall be in its greatest perfection, as one body indeed: the acquaintance and communion of these infants with the other members will be so great and perfect as to give them an ineffable kind of sympathy, in such a manner as will greatly answer instead of experience and, together with the certain knowledge of what has been their own state by nature, will be near akin to consciousness.

4. We don't know how far they will have communicated to them by God a kind of consciousness of that faith that their parents exercised for them.

5. Though elect infants are saved without properly passing through a time of probation and without a personal, actual faith, yet seeing the body

<!-- p. 508 -->

(the church) is saved in consequence of an actual antecedent trial, these forementioned ends are answered, viz. that Christ has the honor of men's being required to receive him on pain of God's peculiar wrath, and there being actually a terrible punishment for rejecting him and neglect and contempt of Christ. And men's giving them [selves] up to sloth and wickedness is not encouraged. And Christ bruises the serpent's head in his own territories and in the same state wherein he ruined man and procured the ignominy and sufferings of Christ, and sets up his kingdom of grace on the ruins of Satan's kingdom, and baffles all Satan's subtlety by his superior wisdom, manifested in the application of redemption and the way in which he carries on the work of actual salvation in the world. And Christ has a glorious victory over Satan in the conversion of sinners. And God shows his faithfulness and the riches and immutability of his love in his continued mercy to his saints, notwithstanding their infirmities. And a proper and wise foundation is laid for a diversity of degrees of glory in heaven, that many of the members of the society shall be higher than others.

[^046-note1]: MS: "respecting."

[^046-note2]: Word supplied by Andover copyist.

[^046-note3]: MS: "taken and."

[^046-note4]: MS: "and."

### 1130 [a]. JUSTIFICATION.

Dr. Manton reconciles the apostle James and the apostle Paul in the following manner, in his *Fifth Volume of Sermons*, p. 274:"Justification hath respect to some accusation. Now as there is a twofold law, there is a two [fold] accusation and justification: the law of works and the law of grace. Now when we are accused as breakers of the law of works, that is, as sinners, obnoxious to the wrath of God, we plead Christ's satisfaction as our righteousness, no works of our own. But when we are accused as non-performers of the conditions of the covenant of grace, as being neglecters and rejecters of Christ the Mediator, we are justified by producing our faith or sincere obedience. So that our righteousness by the new covenant is subordinate to our universal righteousness with respect to the great law of God, and that we have only by Christ. If we are charged that we have broken the first covenant, the covenant of works, we allege Christ's satisfaction and merit; if charged not to have performed the conditions of the law of grace, we answer it by producing our faith, repentance and new obedience, and so show it to be a false charge. Our first and supreme righteousness consists in the pardon of our sins and our acceptance in the Beloved, and our right to impunity and glory; our second and subordinate righteousness in having the true condition of pardon and life. In the first sense, Christ's righteousness is our only justification and righteousness; faith and repentance, or new obedience, is not the least part of it. But in the second, believing, repenting and obeying

<!-- p. 509 -->

is our righteousness in their several respective ways, viz. that the righteousness of Christ may be ours, and continue ours."[^047-note1]

See also Dr. Manton on James, pp. 310–12, 331 ff.[^047-note2]

[^047-note1]: Manton, Sermon 5 on Philippians 3:9, in *A Fifth Volume of Sermons*, p. 274. In the *Complete Works* of 1874, the quote appears in vol. 20, pp. 44–45.

[^047-note2]: Thomas Manton, *A Practical Commentary, or an Exposition with Notes on the Epistle of James* (London, 1651). On pp. 310–12, Manton considers James 2:21 and how Abraham was "justified by works" as opposed to injunctions elsewhere in the New Testament, especially by Paul, which state that justification is by faith alone. Manton seeks to clarify the seeming contradiction by arguing that "*Paul* speaketh of the use and office of faith *in foro Divino*, before God, and *James* speaketh of the effects and qualities of faith, by which it is justified before men." For his willingness to sacrifice Isaac, Abraham's "faith was justified to be right and true" (p. 311). In pp. 331–37, Manton further seeks to reconcile Paul and James on faith and works by asserting "that Obedience is not the *condition* of Justification, but the *evidence*," meaning that righteousness and sanctification go together, thereby showing up the "unjustifiableness of that faith which is without works" (pp. 336–37).

### 1130 [b]. FAITH, how connected with OBEDIENCE.

The very acceptance of Christ in his priestly office, making atonement for sin by his blood and fulfilling the law of God by his perfect obedience unto death, and so the very approbation of the attribute of God as it is thus exhibited, an infinitely holy mercy: I say, merely the soul's acceptance and approbation of these things do thoroughly secure holiness of heart and life in the redeemed of Jesus Christ. They will secure their conformity to the law of God, though by this very mercy and this very Savior they are set at liberty from the law, and are no longer under the law as a law with its sanctions immediately taking hold of them and binding them, binding by its sanctions or threatenings, connecting and binding together its fulfillment and life and its violation and death. Our heart's approving of that holy mercy of God that appears in his showing mercy to sinners—in away of perfectly satisfying the law, suffering all the penalty of it, and of perfectly fulfilling and answering the precepts of it—implies an heart fully approving the law itself as most worthy to be fulfilled and satisfied, approving the authority that established the law, and so his infinite worthiness of being obeyed; in that we approve of it, that so great a person should submit to that authority and do honor to it by becoming a servant to obey God and a sacrifice to satisfy for the contempt done his authority, and that we approve the holy law itself as worthy of such great honor to be done it. It implies a heart entirely detesting sin, and in some sort sensible of the infinite detestableness of it, that we approve of God's making such a manifestation of his detestation of it and approve of the declared fitness and necessity of its [being] punished with so great a punishment as the

<!-- p. 510 -->

sufferings of Christ. Our accepting such sufferings as an atonement for our sin implies a heart fully repenting of and renouncing sin, for it implies not only a conviction that we deserve so great a punishment and not only a mere conviction of conscience, but an approbation of heart of the connection of such sin with such punishment, which implies an hatred of the sin punished. And the heart's entire approbation of such methods perfectly to fulfill the obedience of the law, by so great a person and by his doing so great things and denying himself so much, implies a very high approbation of this law and authority of the Lawgiver. Therefore this acceptance of Christ as a Savior by his obedience and atonement, and an acceptance of God's holy mercy, forgiving sin and giving life in this way, does well secure universal obedience to the law of God as a law of liberty, and with a free and ingenuous spirit, by the obedience of children and not of slaves. Thus the faith that justifies the sinner destroys sin, agreeable to Galatians 2:18. And the heart is purified by faith.

So far as this evangelical spirit prevails, so far fear or a legal spirit will be needless to restrain from sin; and so far will such a legal spirit cease and be driven away.

*Corol*. This which has been observed is a confirmation that this is the true nature of justifying faith, and that the essence of it lies very much in the approbation and acceptance of the heart.

See Mr. Glas' *Notes on Scripture Texts*, No. 3, p. 22.[^048-note1]

[^048-note1]: Glas, *Works, 3*, 134–36. In the "Observes on the Sermon on the Mount," Glas writes that "The Lord Jesus gives the law to his disciples here, in the shape wherein he fulfilled it, or according to the spirit of it, to be observed by them, as the proof and evidence of their being his disciples, his brethren, and so the children of his Father, in distinction from the rest of mankind.… This faith then, must be the principle of the obedience that the Lord here requires of his disciples as the evidence of their being his brethren, the children of his Father… The knowledge of the Son of God is their proper light. This is their light that must shine in their good works to the glory of their father which is in heaven.… If we believe, that our redemption from the curse… is through his being made a curse for us; must not this belief… alienate us from all unrighteousness? and if we believe, that our acceptance with God as his children, is only through his Son's fulfilling the righteousness of this law for us; will not this belief make us have a respect to all these commandments, and influence us to love all his righteousness?"

### 1131. GLORIOUS TIMES. MILLENNIUM. PROGRESS

of the work of redemption. There are yet more glorious times to come. Without doubt that thing, whatsoever it be, that the Scripture represents as a thing wherein that glory of Christ doth much consist, which shall be given him as the reward of his labors and sufferings, shall be accomplished in a very high degree. The accomplishment shall not fall short of the representations and

<!-- p. 511 -->

promises. The reward God will give his dear Son for such a service as he did will doubtless be great indeed, and the promises of these rewards shall be fulfilled to the utmost. But the great number of those that shall be redeemed by Christ is very often in Scripture spoken of as one thing wherein much of that glory of Christ shall consist, which shall be given him in reward for his labors and sufferings. Solomon says, Proverbs 14:28, "In the multitude of people is the king's honor." And 'tis often promised that Christ should have honor in his kingdom in this world far above all other kings; that God would make him his first born, higher than the kings of the earth; that God would give him the heathen for his inheritance and the utmost parts of the earth for his possession; that his people should be willing in the day of his power; that his redeemed ones should be numerous as the drops of dew; that his kingdom should break in pieces all other kingdoms standing in opposition to it and grow great and fill the whole earth; that there should be given to him dominion, glory and a kingdom; that all people, nations and languages should serve him; that every knee should bow and every tongue confess to him, and all the ends of the earth should look to him and be saved.

It was often spoken of in the Old Testament as a great honor and privilege of the father of a family or head of a progeny or race to have a numerous posterity. Psalms 127:3–5, "Lo, children are the heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: they shall not be ashamed, they shall speak with the enemies in the gate." This was often promised to the patriarchs as a great evidence of God's favor. Genesis 13:16, "And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth: so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then shall thy seed also be numbered." Genesis 15:5, "Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars […]: and he said, so shall thy seed be." And Genesis 22:17, "That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore." So to Isaac, Genesis 26:4, "And I will make thy seed to multiply as the stars of heaven." And to Jacob, Genesis 28:14, "And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, to the north, and to the south." Genesis 32:12, "I will surely do thee good, and make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude." And 'tis observable that these very promises to the patriarchs relate to the multitude of Christ's seed.

'Tis spoken of in Balaam's blessing of Israel as a great part of their privilege and blessedness, that their number should be exceeding great.

<!-- p. 512 -->

Numbers 23:10, "Who can count the dust of Jacob, and number the fourth part of Israel?" And so 'tis expressly spoken as a great part of the honor and reward that God will give to Christ for his making his soul an offering for sin, that he should see his seed, should see of the travail of his soul, and be satisfied.

### 1132. CHRIST'S RESURRECTION.

That Christ should not manifest himself to others besides his disciples after his resurrection, and that he should not be constantly with them day and night, living in their manner but that he should only manifest himself to them now and then and then disappear in the manner that he did, may be accounted for thus: for him to have done otherwise would have been to have continued his state of humiliation. If he had still lived by meat, drink and sleep with the disciples and dwelt and traveled and conversed constantly with them, then he must have accommodated in many respects to their state in this world. And that would not [have] been consistent with the finishing of his humiliation at his resurrection. And if he had frequently exposed himself to the view of his enemies and the multitude promiscuously instead of certain chosen persons, he would still have continued to expose himself to reproach and the ill treatment of the world, which would have been yet more inconsistent with an end to his humiliation at his resurrection.

### 1133. WISDOM OF GOD IN THE WORK OF REDEMPTION. DAY OF JUDGMENT. PROGRESS OF THE WORK [OF] REDEMPTION.

The great majesty and glory and exceeding purity and holiness in which the Judge will appear at the day of judgment, which will so terrify the wicked and manifest their exceeding guiltiness to their own consciences and to the world, will but the more[^051-note1] establish and heighten the confidence of the saints and every way confirm and advance their joy. The sight of that awful and pure glory will the more clearly demonstrate their perfect freedom from guilt, for it will demonstrate the value and sufficiency of the atonement that has been made for them, as it will show the dignity and excellency of the high priest and sacrifice by which atonement was made. For this was no other than that same person that then will appear so great and glorious. He made atonement by the sacrifice of himself. The glory in which he will then appear will show the preciousness of his blood and its sufficiency to atone for the most heinous sins. And that will also demonstrate the value of his righteousness and tend to make 'em the more confident in appearing in

<!-- p. 513 -->

it before the judgment seat. The sight of his glory will convince of his sufficiency and excellency as a Mediator in all respects.

The great appearances and manifestations that will be of Christ's power, such as the earth's being removed, the universe shaken to pieces and the like, which will so terrify the ungodly, will only increase the confidence of the saints, as they hereby will see how strong their rock and refuge is. And the sight of that flaming fire and those dreadful manifestations of wrath with which he shall appear will not terrify them; they will only increase the sense of his love to them. For the greatest testimonies of wrath shall be against their enemies, the devil and wicked persecutors of the churMatthew 25:42, "I was an hungered, and ye gave me no meat," etc. So that, really, the most awful manifestations of the Judge's wrath will be manifestations of the exceeding greatness of his love to the saints. All will show that they are as the apple of his eye. And then the saints shall be admitted to join with Christ in judging these enemies and shall be as it were with him in executing this vengeance, in breaking these enemies with a rod of iron.

[^051-note1]: MS: "most."

### 1134. HEAVEN

the everlasting abode of the church. That the saints shall enter into heaven after the day of judgment and not continue with Christ here below is evident by John 14:2–3, "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also." Doubtless these words, "I will come again, and receive you to myself; that where I am," etc., will be most eminently fulfilled at Christ's second coming at the end of the world, that second coming spoken of, Hebrews 9:28, "So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation." And when it is said he will receive them to himself to be where he is, he must be understood [as saying], "To the place to which I am now go[ing], to that house of my Father to which I am ascended, in which I am going to prepare a place for you; at my second coming I will receive [you] to those mansions that I now go to prepare in my Father's house."

'Tis also evident by Hebrews 6:20, "Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest forever after the order of Melchizedec." 'Tis evident that Christ went to the highest heavens—the third heaven, far above all heavens—at his first ascension as the forerunner of his people, implying that they shall all go there in their turn or after him. And doubtless in this he was the forerunner of them with respect

<!-- p. 514 -->

to their reception of their proper reward, or their complete happiness, which will not be till the last day; and their forerunner as to a bodily ascension or translation, wherein the saints' bodies shall be made like to Christ's glorious body and shall ascend as that did. But they will not have glorified bodies till then. And he is doubtless the forerunner of the whole church in going to heaven, which he would not be if, after the day of judgment, the saints were to stay here below. For those which shall then be found alive in such a case never would ascend into heaven at all. And then 'tis most reasonable to suppose that Christ will be the firstfruits in his ascension in like manner as in his resurrection. But Christ is the firstfruits in his resurrection with regard to what the saints shall be the subjects of at the second coming of Christ. 1 Corinthians 15:23, "Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ's at his coming."

### 1135. FUTURE STATE.

The most eminent exercises and manifestations of virtue are undoubtedly those that are attended with the greatest self-denial. But if there be no future state, such virtue as this will be furthest from a reward. When men in this world deny themselves most in their course of virtue, they would be the greatest losers. For, by the supposition, they fare hardest at present; otherwise, they would not go most contrary to their present ease, pleasure or interest, and so would not deny themselves most.

### 1136. INFINITE EVIL OF SIN.

The following is taken from Dr. Manton, in the fifth volume of his *Sermons*, p. 411:"There is this difference between sin and obedience, that the heinousness of sin is always aggravated and heightened by the proportion of the object, but the merit and value of obedience is still lessened. The sin or offense is aggravated; as to strike an officer is more than to strike a private man, a king more than an ordinary officer. Thence it cometh to pass that sin committed against God doth deserve an infinite punishment, because the majesty of God is infinite; and so eternal death is the wages of sin. But on the other side, the value or merit of obedience is lessened. The greater God is, and the more glorious his Being, the greater obligation lieth upon us to love and serve him; and the good which we do for his sake being wholly due to him, God is not bound by any right or justice from the merit of the action itself to reward it: for here the greatness of the object lesseneth the action or respect thereby performed to it (Luke 17:10). For the creature oweth itself to God, who made it, and enabled it to do [all] that it can do; so that he is not bound to reward it out of his natural justice, but inclined to do it out

<!-- p. 515 -->

of his own goodness, and bound to do it by his free promise and gracious covenant."[^054-note1]

[^054-note1]: Manton, Sermon 3 on 2 Thessalonians 1:6–7, in *A Fifth Volume of Sermons*, p. 411. In the *Complete Works* of 1874, the quote appears in vol. 20, p. 221.

### 1137. HAPPINESS OF HEAVEN. When God had finished the work of creation, he is represented as resting and being refreshed and rejoicing in his works. The Apostle compares the happiness Christ entered into, after he had finished his labors and sufferings in the work of redemption, to this (Hebrews 4:4, Hebrews 4:10). Therefore we may well suppose that very much of Christ's happiness in heaven consists in beholding the glory of God appearing in the work of redemption, and so in rejoicing in his own work and reaping the sweet fruit of it, the glorious success of it, which was the joy that was set before him. And as the Apostle represents the future happiness of the saints by a participation of God's rest and Christ's rest from their works (Hebrews 4:4–11; see note on Hebrews 4:5, "Blank Bible"), this seems to argue two things: viz. 1. that the way that the saints will be happy in the beholding the glory of God will be very much in beholding the glory of his perfections in his works; 2. that the happiness of the saints in heaven, especially since Christ's ascension, consisting in beholding God's glory, will consist very much in seeing his glory in the work of redemption. The happiness of departed saints under the old testament consisted much in beholding the glory of God in the works of creation, in the beholding which the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy. But their happiness since Christ's ascension consists much more in beholding the glory of God in the work of redemption, since that the old creation in comparison of this is no more mentioned nor comes into mind, but they will be glad and rejoice forever in this work. The beatifical vision of God in heaven consists mostly in beholding the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, either in his work or in his person as appearing in the glorified human nature. PROGRESS OF THE WORK OF REDEMPTION.

[^055-note1]

 

[^055-note1]: JE cites p. 857 of the "Blank Bible," which falls in the middle of commentary on I Timothy. In the note on Hebrews 4:5, he points out that "In the expression of MY REST, the Apostle plainly understands… the rest that God himself enjoys." The Apostle therefore, according to JE, is here exhorting Christians "to seek to be partakers of the rest that Christ enjoys, that he entered into when he finished and ceased from his works."

### 1138. REASONS to think that the gracious SINCERITY of our neighbors is a thing which, as to its certain knowledge, is altogether UNSEARCHABLE BY MEN:

 

<!-- p. 516 -->

That the devil seeks to destroy men and bring 'em to final apostasy after their conversion, as he did Peter.

That it [is] so often spoken of as a high prerogative of God to search the heart with respect to this matter.

That some that have been reckoned among the most eminent by the church of God in a very enlightened state have proved apostates, as Nicolas the deacon [Acts 6:5].

That the Apostle commands that a novice or new convert should not be made a bishop, lest being lifted up with pride he should fall into the condemnation of the devil, i.e. through pride should prove an apostate.

That it is so much spoken of as so great a work of God to try men and prove whether they are indeed sincere in his dealings with them, and so great and high an act of his, [an] act of the judge of the world, at the last day to make men manifest by their works.

That God himself, speaking of himself after the manner of men (i.e. doubtless after the manner of wise and good men), speaks of himself as trusting the profession and appearance of hypocrites and being deceived thereby.

That the falling away of false professors is so often in Ezekiel called the falling of righteous men from their righteousness [Ezekiel 3:20; Ezekiel 18:24, Ezekiel 18:26; Ezekiel 33:18]. They are called righteous men just in the same manner as true saints are.[^056-note1]

[^056-note1]: In the MS, JE left half of the next page empty, most likely to provide further space for adding to No. 1138.

### 1139. TYPES.

That some things in the Old Testament are types of gospel things and so are intended for our instruction, which are nowhere explained in the New Testament, is evident by Hebrews 9:4–5, "Which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid round about with gold, wherein was the golden pot that had manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant; and over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercy seat; of which" (or, "of which things") "we cannot now speak particularly," i.e. we cannot now particularly explain what gospel or heavenly things they signified (see Hebrews 9:8, Hebrews 9:9, Hebrews 9:23, Hebrews 9:24); in like manner as he had said before, Hebrews 5:10–11, "after the order of Melchizedek. Of whom we have many things to say."

### 1140. END OF THE CREATION, etc. GLORY OF GOD.

The main argument that many modern divines [use] against God's making his own glory his

<!-- p. 517 -->

last end in his works comes only to this: that God is self-sufficient and infinitely happy in himself and therefore can't be gratified in the creatures' beholding and admiring his glory and loving and honoring him for it, because to be gratified or take any pleasure in this would argue that he receives an accession of happiness. But infinite and all-sufficient happiness can receive no accession. But this argument is not properly against God's being gratified or taking pleasure in being glorified amongst his creatures, as against his being gratified or taking pleasure in anything whatsoever pertaining to the creature, and is as much an argument against his taking pleasure in the happiness of his creatures, or in seeing his creatures happy, as his taking pleasure in their beholding his glory and glorifying him for it; when indeed if the matter be justly considered and explained, the supposing of neither of these argues any insufficiency or need in God. He don't take pleasure in either of them because he receives anything from the creature, but because he takes pleasure in what is worthy and eligible in itself considered. He delights in the communications of his own happiness because 'tis a thing valuable and desirable in itself that some communications of his happiness should be made and enjoyed. So he takes pleasure in his glories being manifested and respected because this is a thing fit and amiable in itself, that his glory should be manifested and respected.

### 1142. GLORY OF GOD. END OF THE CREATION.

[^059-note1]

See No. 1066, and No. 1082. That glory of God that is spoken of in Scripture as the end of God's works is the egress and reception of God's fullness, the egress of it from God and the reception of it by the creature. The fullness of God is twofold: 'tis his excellency and his happiness, answerable hereto. There is a twofold faculty in the creature that the egress has respect to and which is its recipient subject, viz. a faculty of perceiving and of approving; a twofold manner of egress or going forth, viz. manifestation and communication.

There are three things called by the name of glory in Scripture: excellency, goodness and happiness.

[^059-note1]: There is no No. 1141.

### 1143. CONVICTION. PREPARATORY WORK.

There is very commonly that difference between such souls as are of the generation of the upright, and born and brought up in thoroughly religious families, and others, as to the new birth, that may be compared to the difference which was between the Hebrew women and the Egyptian women with respect to their travail in the natural birth of their children.

<!-- p. 518 -->

### 1144. INSPIRATION. PROPHECY.

That the prophets, after they had once had intercourse with God by immediate revelation from God, gained acquaintance with [him] so as afterwards to know him, as it were to know his voice or know what was indeed a revelation from God, is confirmed by 1 Samuel 3:7.

### 1145. SATISFACTION OF CHRIST.

Christ's knowing his own infinite dignity and glory and having it in view in the time of his humiliation is mentioned as a circumstance that is important and of great consequence in that humiliation (John 13:3–4).

### 1146. CHRIST'S RIGHTEOUSNESS, OBEDIENCE, SUFFERINGS.

Christ speaks of his obedience as chiefly consisting in his voluntary undergoing [of] his last sufferings and as a great manifestation of his love to the Father, and the end of his sufferings being his openly honoring God by such a manifestation of his love, in John 14:30–31. "Hereafter I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me. But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do."

### 1147. MORAL EVIL

consisting in something negative. ORIGINAL SIN. Because moral evil consists in what is negative, therefore it is often called in Scripture by the name of vanity or emptiness, and that good which is opposite to it is called fullness. See note on Genesis 1:2 and Ephesians 3:19.

### 1148. ABOLISHING THE CEREMONIAL LAW.

'Tis very manifest that if the state and circumstances of God's people were so altered that the institutions of Mosaic law did not agree thereto, but it was necessary that they should be altered to accommodate their circumstance, this was a proper occasion for setting aside those laws, and particularly if there were need of this to accommodate the multitude of worshippers and the services they had to offer. This appears from what Solomon did, that we have an account of, 1 Kings 8:64, "The same day did the king hallow the middle of the court that was before the house of the Lord: for there he offered burnt offerings, and meat offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings: because the brazen altar that was before the Lord was too little to receive the burnt offerings, and meat offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings." It was strictly enjoined in the law of Moses that the people should offer their sacrifices only on the altar of the Lord that was before the sanctuary (Exodus 20:24–25). And from time to time it is commanded that the sacrifices

<!-- p. 519 -->

should be offered on the altar,[^065-note1] and the offering sacrifice anywhere else is threatened even with cutting off from among their people (Leviticus 17:8–9). And how jealous were the children of Israel when they supposed that the two tribes and half had built another altar for sacrifice besides the altar of the Lord. But yet when there was occasion by reason of the multitude of people and of sacrifices, another place is made use of, and that just after the altar had been built vastly larger than that which had been used before. And what Solomon did then was attended with all manner of tokens of the divine acceptance. See the history, 1 Kings 8, 2 Chronicles 6-7.

And this law of offering sacrifices only on that altar was also often set aside on other occasion by God's special direction to offer sacrifices elsewhere; for instance, the altar that Joshua built at Mt. Ebal (Joshua 8:30) and the altar that Gideon built and the sacrifices he offered upon it (Judges 6:24 ff.), and the sacrifice that Manoah offered on a rock (Judges 13:19–20) and the altar that Elijah built (1 Kings 18:30 ff.).

See Bp. Kidder's *Demonstration*, Pt. III, pp. 3–27.[^065-note2]

Samuel's wearing a linen ephod and officiating as a priest—who, though a Levite, was not of the posterity of Aaron—was a departing from the ceremonial law; so his offering a sucking lamb (1 Samuel 7:9).

[^065-note1]: The remainder of the sentence is a later addition, written in a black ink similar to that used to write the additions at the end of the entry and characteristic of the 1750s.

[^065-note2]: This reference and the following paragraph in this entry are later additions. Kidder, *Demonstration of the Messias*, Pt. III, ch. 1, considers "Another great pretence of the Jews, and prejudice against Christianity, ariseth from an opinion, which they hold pertinaciously, that the law of Moses is of perpetual obligation" (p. 1). Beginning at p. 3, Kidder distinguishes between the perpetual moral law and "positive institutions," both ceremonial and political. The latter type is not of perpetual obligation because 1) "they are not good in themselves," 2) they were "never intended for the whole world" but only for one people, 3) they ceased with the coming of the Messiah and the calling of the Gentiles, 4) some Jews themselves asserted that the Mosaic law was not indispensable, 5) God forewarned that the institutions of Moses would end in the days of the Messiah, and 6) God never declared that the institutions of Moses were to stand forever.

### 1150.

[^066-note1]

<!-- p. 520 -->

THE FAITH OF MIRACLES

was not properly a distinct sort of faith from other faith. I can see no reason from the Scripture to imagine so. The particular revelation that was the ground of it was different. Promises or revelations made to different persons may be different. But it does not necessarily follow that the faith by which these different revelations are believed or relied on are therefore different sorts of faith.

They were many different revelations that were the grounds of the faith, mentioned in the various parts of Hebrews 11. It is one revelation that we have—that the worlds were made by the word of God—that that faith depends on, spoken of, Hebrews 11:3. The revelation that the world should be destroyed by a flood and that Noah should be saved in an ark—that Noah's faith relied on—was another revelation. And the revelation made to Abraham—that God would make him a great nation and that all the families of the earth should be blessed in him—that his faith relied on, was another revelation. And the revelation that Isaac had concerning Jacob's and Esau's posterity—by which he blessed them concerning things to come—was a different revelation.[^066-note2] And that faith by which the walls of Jericho fell down, that was in another revelation. But because these revelations, relied on by the various examples of faith mentioned in this chapter, [were different],[^066-note3] it does not therefore follow that each one had a different sort of faith.

The faith of miracles was a faith in a revelation made by God to the person that God made use of in working the miracle. God evermore gave some intimation of his mind and will to the person that was called to act as the instrument. Neither Moses, nor Joshua, nor Elijah, nor any of the prophets pretended to work miracles of their own hands, what they pleased and when they pleased; it was only what God pleased and when he pleased.

Moses says, Numbers 16:28, "Hereby ye shall know that the Lord hath sent me to do all these works; for I have not done them of mine own mind." And Elijah says, 1 Kings 18:36, "Let it be known this day that thou art God in Israel, and that I am thy servant, and that I have done all these things at thy word." These are the two chief of the old testament prophets for working of miracles.

And therefore it was every way fit and suitable and necessary that the person that God so much honored as to make use of him as the instrument of working the miracle should therein act with a respect to God as the author of the miracle, as the being that wrought [it] by his own power and sufficiency and of his own will. But for the instrument thus (in what he does in the affair) to have respect to God as the author of the miracle, as working it by his own will and power, is the same thing as to act in faith

<!-- p. 521 -->

in God, or in a dependence on his power and sufficiency and[^066-note4] some revelation or signification of his mind and will. Seeing the instrument is really nothing in the affair, but the work truly is wholly God's and the instrument a mere instrument without any power or will of his own in the case, hence 'tis suitable and highly requisite that he should act as in the name of the Lord. It is requisite that he should do so visibly, and not take upon him to work miracles as of his own power and authority, as Christ did. And since God sees the heart and looks at that, 'tis requisite that he should not only visibly act as in the name of the Lord, but really and internally, in the act of his mind. But this is the same thing as to act in faith in God and in a dependence on him. Otherwise he don't really act in His name, but in his own name; he don't worship God in working the miracle, but makes a god of himself.

God is pleased often to make use of men as instruments in working miracles. But when he makes use of intelligent voluntary agents in such an affair, he will use 'em in a manner that is agreeable to their nature, not as senseless, lifeless instruments.

But to make use of rational intelligent creatures as instruments in a manner agreeable to their intelligent nature is to make a proper use of their intelligent faculties in the affair. But the use that is made of their intelligent voluntary faculties can't be a producing the miracle through the efficiency of those faculties as being employed themselves to produce [it]. Therefore it can be nothing else than as [being] employed in, looking to, acknowledging, and depending on that Being by whose power and will the miracle is indeed wrought.

God sometimes made use of brute creatures as instruments to do his work. So he made use of the two she-bears to punish the children that mocked Elisha. Sometimes he makes use of things without life. So he made use of the stones he sent down from heaven to destroy the Amorites. But it is not thus that he makes use of intelligent, voluntary, spiritual creatures, or human souls or minds, to work miracles. Indeed, they cannot properly and in strictness of speech be instruments at all, for a miracle is wrought by the immediate power of God. What they do has really no proper efficiency at all in the case, as tools have that men work with. Their acts are truly no more than circumstances of the miracle. It pleases God for wise ends to work the miracle with such acts of theirs as the antecedent and concomitant circumstances and appendages of the work. But the acts of those human minds or intelligent beings that God is pleased to make

<!-- p. 522 -->

to be the antecedent and attending circumstances of the work are proper exercises of understanding and will towards him as the author of the miracle. But these are the same as acts of faith in him. Created minds can be made use of as the instruments of miracles in no higher sense than that God should annex the miracle to proper acts of those minds towards him as the author, so that the mind shall as it were go to God for the effect and bring it down from him.

Because it is so suitable and requisite that men that God makes use [of] in working miracles should, in order to it, act faith in God as the author of the miracle, hence the prayer of those that were [made] use of to God, for the miracle wrought, so commonly preceded the miracle. For prayer is only the expression of faith. And hence Christ, when he encouraged his disciples to act faith in God in order to their working miracles, he from time to time told 'em that whatsoever they should ask of God, believing, they should receive.

But in order clearly to understand the nature of the faith of miracles, the following things may be noted:

1. It was with the faith of miracles as it was with other faith, in this respect: that it implied a conviction and satisfaction of mind concerning the divine sufficiency and faithfulness in general, i.e. a full and satisfying conviction that God is able to do whatsoever he pleases and that he is immutably true in all that he promises or reveals; and also a dependence on a revelation or signification God has given of his mind with respect to that particular thing that God is depended upon for.

2. The revelation or signification of God's mind that the prophets, apostles and others depended [on] in working miracles was either express or only implicit. Oftentimes before the miracle wrought, when God called the person to be made use of to perform such and such acts, he did at the same time expressly declare that, on the performance of them, such and such a miracle should ensue. So it was with many of the miracles of Moses and Joshua, and with respect to many of the miracles of the prophets and apostles that are recorded in Scripture, where is no express mention of an express promise or revelation made by God beforehand that, on their performing such acts, the miracle should ensue. Yet there [is] all reason to think that this was indeed the case, that the persons improved had an inward intimation of the mind of God, or what God would do by inspiration or by the word of the Lord's coming to 'em (as the expression often is in Scripture), which intimation it was their duty fully to rely upon, not doubting in the least but that God would verify his word in doing the work

<!-- p. 523 -->

revealed, however strange it appeared, though it were as wonderful as a mountain's removing from its ancient base into the midst of the sea, or bringing water out of a rock. To have the least hesitancy of faith in such a case would be a great sin, as it was in Moses at the waters of Meribah.

Sometimes 'tis probable the revelation was not express, but only implicit. The revelation was not in the form of an express promise or declaration that God would, on their performing such acts, produce such a miracle. But it was only a signification of God's will by revelation in the manner of a command or direction to go and perform such and such actions or speak such words in order to such a miracle following, which implied in it a promise that, if they did so in an acknowledgment of his sufficiency and faithfulness and dependence thereon, the miracle should follow. In such a case it was their duty, without hesitation or doubting, to go and perform the acts required, though it were never so publicly, and though they pawned all their credit on the success of their attempt.

3. The revelation that the persons improved acted faith in, might be either particular or only general. God oftentimes, by some particular revelation, directed the prophets to go and do such and such things in a dependence on him in order to such a particular miracle's being wrought, with a promise either express or implicit, or his concurring almighty power. Or it might be only general, as when Christ sent forth his disciples to work such and such miracles on all proper occasions for the confirming of their doctrine; which is all the express command that needs to be supposed, the Spirit of God thenceforward working in them only as a Spirit of wisdom, guiding of them with respect to proper occasions. This was implicitly promised to the apostles when he sent 'em forth before his passion, but especially when they were sent forth after his resurrection. These things together were equivalent to a particular and express revelation with respect to each particular miracle, affording an equal foundation and obligation for faith in God with respect to all miracles they were called to work.

4. The revelation or promise that was made to him that was improved as the instrument in working a miracle, and that he had to depend on, was a conditional promise or declaration suspended on certain acts of his. If it were suspended on no acts of his, then he would not be in any respect an instrument in it. For therein does his instrumentality lie, viz. in the connection of the event on his acts. These acts of the instrument that the promise was suspended on were twofold: first, inward, or the act of the mind, which was in the exercise of dependence on God's sufficiency and

<!-- p. 524 -->

faithfulness; secondly, those outward acts that he was to perform in signification of those acts of the mind, such as prayer or certain words to be spoken (as those of Peter, Acts 3:6, "In the name of Jesus Christ, rise up and walk") or actions to be performed, as laying hands on the sick, anointing with oil, etc.

5. As the faith of miracles was no different sort of faith from other faith (though the revelation it relied on was different), so it has the same distinctions as other faith (or faith in other revelations) has. As there is a special or spiritual and [a] common faith in the revelation that God has made of himself in the gospel to mankind in general, so there was a spiritual and a common faith of miracles, or in those particular revelations or significations of God's mind made to the persons that were called to work miracles. A person might have the latter to a high [degree] and not the former. And God was pleased sometimes to succeed a common faith so as to cause the miracle to ensue. Thus a man might have faith so as to remove mountains, and yet have no charity.

Not that I suppose that there was any proper promise made of such success to only a common faith. But God was often pleased to reward this common faith with such success, this honor and privilege of being instruments of working miracles being but a common blessing and not one of those things that belong to or accompany salvation. God therefore rewarded this common faith, as he is wont often to reward other common graces and moral virtues, with temporal and common rewards. And the common faith of many was succeeded to work miracles in a course for a long time and, it may be, sometimes as long as life lasted. But yet this success was uncertain. God was not obliged to bestow 'em, as it is with all kinds of benefits that are not secured by the promises of the covenant of grace and are not some of the sure mercies of David. That in Matthew 21:21–22 and other parallel promises are not made to anything but to a true spiritual faith and prayer.

6. Inasmuch as the faith of miracles was not properly any different sort of faith from other faith, so the faith of miracles was not itself properly miraculous or what was wrought in any more extraordinary manner than other faith (at least it was not always so). Hence the faith of miracles was as much the duty of the person called to work miracles as any other faith. And when they failed of it, they greatly sinned. Hence Christ blames his disciples for want of faith when they could not cure the demoniac brought to 'em while he was in the mount of transfiguration. And hence God was angry with Moses for his want of faith in working that miracle of bringing water out of the rock.

### 1151. END OF THE CREATION.

[^067-note1]

See No. 1066. It is no just objection against God's aiming at glorifying himself—as one way of that flowing out or beaming forth of the infinite good that is to [be] considered under the notion of a last end of God's works—that this adds nothing to God's happiness, any more than it is a just objection against his communication [of] his happiness to his creatures being aimed at by him as his last end. For creatures' happiness does not properly add anything to God's happiness, any more than God's being glorified in the view of the creature and by the creature adds something to God's happiness. It is true, God delights in communicating his happiness to the creature, as therein he exercises a perfection of his nature and does that which is condecent, amiable, and beautiful, and so enjoys himself and his own perfection in it, as his perfection is exercised in it. So, in like manner, he delights in glorifying himself, as it is in itself condecent and beautiful that infinite brightness and glory should shine forth, and it is a part of the perfection of God to seek it.

These two ways of the divine good beaming forth are agreeable to the two ways of the divine essence flowing out or proceeding from eternity within the Godhead in the person of the Son and Holy Spirit: the one in an expression of his glory, in the idea or knowledge of it; the other the flowing out of the essence in love and joy. It is condecent that, correspondent to these proceedings of the divinity *ad intra*, God should also flow forth *ad extra*.

The one last end of all things may be expressed thus: it is that the infinite good might be communicated, that it might be communicated to, or rather in, the understandings of the creature, which communication is God's declarative glory; and that it might be communicated to the other faculty, usually (though not very expressively) called the will; which is the making the creature happy in God as a partaker of God's happiness.

[^067-note1]: "Miscellanies" No. 1151 is missing from the original MS; the text is supplied from the Andover copy.

### 1152. COVENANTS. PERFECT OBEDIENCE. CHRIST'S RIGHTEOUSNESS.

The original MS resumes here. The part of the original MS page on which JE wrote No. 1152 (as well as a brief section of No. 1150) was cut out at some point; the fragment is now at the Library of Congress.

So it is most natural to understand that [saying] of Christ, John 12:50, "And I know that his commandment is life everlasting," that obedience to the commands of God the Father is the grand, unalterable condition of eternal life to all his subjects universally. See the context.
